newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Paris bank staff won't release hostage boss.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Paris bank staff won't release hostage boss.

text.p: A government-appointed mediator on Tuesday sought the release of the chairman of Credit Foncier de France, held for the fifth day in a siege of the state-owned bank's headquarters by hundreds of staff.
But union representatives held out against his request at a gathering inside the bank building straight after meeting with mediator Philippe Rouvillois.
"Nothing should happen as long as we're still in an active phase of this (mediation) mission," CFTC union representative Agnes Courtoux told a staff general assembly.

Rouvillois said the release of chairman Jerome Meyssonnier was not a pre-condition for the start of any negotiations with staff, who are protesting against a government plan to wind down the financially troubled property lender.

"I did not use the term pre-condition because that sounds like an ultimatum and I believe that the role of a conciliator is not to set ultimatums," Rouvillois said after he met union representatives for an hour of talks.

"But in fact, I believe it (the liberation) is a condition to allow a climate in which we can work fruitfully," he added. For the unions, Daniel Perrin said after the meeting that the talks were "brief but constructive".

Meysonnier and seven of his colleagues have been held in the bank offices since Friday afternoon, but, after taking a more conciliatory stance initially, said on Monday he considered himself a hostage.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe intervened on Monday to appoint Rouvillois to try to break the deadlock with unions who argue that the bank could be made viable and should be kept intact.

Hundreds of employees were occupying the central lobby of the plush Paris headquarters on Tuesday, many of them having spent yet another night sprawled across the marble floor of the giant atrium in sleeping bags.

Finance Minister Jean Arthuis announced in July that part of the debt-laden group would be spun off to another cooperatively run group called Credit Immobilier, which would take on 1,500 of the staff, with the rest shunted into a new state holding company that would be closed down gradually.

But he is now facing blanket media coverage of the plight of some 3,300 staff at a time of record unemployment and the thorny task of sorting out a bank which was set up by Emperor Napoleon III 145 years ago and has a long history of providing low-cost housing loans to France's poorer families.

Arthuis, questioned in the National Assembly on Tuesday by parliamentarians from his own camp in the centre-right government, said Credit Foncier had been involved in a series of "misadventures" and could not survive alone.
"I don't think taxpayers should have to foot the bill for yet another state bank," he told the lower house of parliament.

Staff taking part in the occupation are being helped by employees from around the country to keep the vigil going. Keen to keep public opinion on their side, the staff have also made sure branches of Credit Foncier remained open for business.
